DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93, Module 4.

Terminal objective

1.0 Given a block diagram, print, or schematic, IDENTIFY the basic component symbols as presented in this module. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.v

Enabling objectives

1.1 IDENTIFY the symbols used on engineering electronic block diagrams, prints, and schematics, for the following components. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.v

  • a. Fixed resistor
  • b. Variable resistor
  • c. Tapped resistor
  • d. Fixed capacitor
  • e. Variable capacitor
  • f. Fixed inductor
  • g. Variable inductor
  • h. Diode
  • i. Light emitting diode (LED)
  • j. Ammeter
  • k. Voltmeter
  • l. Wattmeter
  • m. Chassis ground
  • n. Circuit ground
  • o. Fuse
  • p. Plug
  • q. Headset
  • r. Light bulb
  • s. Silicon controlled rectifier (SCR)
  • t. Half wave rectifier
  • u. Full wave rectifier
  • v. Oscillator
  • w. Potentiometer
  • x. Rheostat
  • y. Antenna
  • z. Amplifier
  • aa. PNP and NPN transistors
  • bb. Junction

Two kinds of electronic prints

Objectives 1.2

"Electronic prints fall into two basic categories, electronic schematics and block diagrams." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.1
"Electronic schematics represent the most detailed category of electronic drawings." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.1
"They depict every component in a circuit, the component's technical information (such as its ratings), and how each component is wired into the circuit." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.1
"Block diagrams are the simplest type of drawing." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.1

A block diagram shows any part, component, or system as a simple geometric shape. One block can stand for a single component, such as a relay, or an entire system. The intended use of the drawing sets the level of detail. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.1

"A block diagram presents the flow or functional information about a circuit, but it is not a detailed depiction of the circuit." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.17
"An electronic schematic diagram presents the detailed information about the circuit, each of its components, and how they are wired into the circuit." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.17

Electronic symbols

Objectives 1.1

"Figure 1 and Figure 2 illustrate the most common electronic symbols used on electronic schematics." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.2
  • Meters: a circle marked A for ammeter, V for voltmeter, or W for wattmeter
  • Oscillator: listed with A/C source in a meter style circle
  • Diode: an arrowhead against a bar
  • Light emitting diode: a diode with arrows pointing away
  • Amplifier: a triangle
  • Antenna: a Y or a V shape on a line
  • Junction: a dot where conductors connect

DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.4

Schematics are the hardest drawings to read, because they require knowing how each component affects, or is affected by, an electrical current. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.2

"This type of drawing provides the level of information needed to troubleshoot electronic circuits." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.2

Schematic and pictorial layout

Objectives 1.0

"The schematics do not show placement or scale, merely function and flow." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.5

A second type, the pictorial layout diagram, is less a schematic than a picture of how the circuit actually looks. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.5

"These drawings show the actual layout of the components on the circuit board." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.5

It is a two-dimensional drawing, usually looking down from the top, and normally comes with a parts list. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.5

Finding power and ground

Objectives 1.0

Reading a print means identifying the condition of the components and following the events as the circuit functions. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.7

"As with electrical systems, the relays and contacts shown are always in the de-energized condition." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.7

Modern electronic systems usually have few, if any, relays or contacts. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.7

"The first observation in dealing with a detailed electronic schematic is the source and polarity of power." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.7

Power is generally shown either as an input transformer or as a numerical value. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.7

"In this convention, dots on the primary and secondary indicate current flow into the primary and out of the secondary at a given instant of time." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.7

The power source is generally stated at the point it enters the schematic, with polarity, such as +15 volts or -15 volts. These markings are usually at the top and bottom of schematics, but not always. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.7

"Unless specified as an Alternating Current (AC) power source, the voltages can normally be assumed to be Direct Current (DC)." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.7
"In any circuit, a ground must be established to create a complete current path." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.8

The direction of current flow can be found from the polarity of the power supplies. When polarities are shown, ground may not always be shown. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.8

Transistors and diodes

Objectives 1.1

The transistor and the diode are the most common semiconductor devices. A semiconductor will be one of two varieties, the PNP or NPN. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.8

The direction of the arrow indicates the type. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.9

Only the common emitter configuration is shown here. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.9

"Using conventional current flow (i.e. from + to -), current will travel through the transistor from most positive to least positive and in the direction of the arrow on the emitter." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.9
"If the input is also positive, the transistor will conduct." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.9
"If the input goes negative, as in Figure 8, the conduction of the device stops because the input, or in this case the base junction, controls the transistor condition." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.9
"The same rules apply as above except that this time polarities of power must change to allow current flow." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.10
"However, diodes are simpler than transistors because they have only one junction and conduct in only one direction, as indicated in Figure 10." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.10
"The diode symbol, like the transistor symbol, shows the direction of conduction by the direction of the arrow, which is from positive to negative." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.10

Knowledge check: Transistors and diodes

Objective 1.1Q1257

An NPN transistor has a positive supply and ground on the emitter. The input goes negative. What happens?

The answer is C. If the input goes negative, the conduction of the device stops because the base junction controls the transistor condition. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.9

Report a problem
Objective 1.1Q1258

Which way does the arrow on a diode symbol point?

The answer is D. The diode symbol shows the direction of conduction by the direction of the arrow, which is from positive to negative. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.10

Report a problem
Objective 1.1Q1259

Why is a diode simpler than a transistor?

The answer is A. Diodes are simpler than transistors because they have only one junction and conduct in only one direction. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.10

Bistables and continuing a circuit

Objectives 1.0

"In most cases, bistables will be indicated by a box or circle, as shown in Figure 11 (A)." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.11

The lines in or around bistables mark them as bistables and also show how they function. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.11

One circuit often connects to other circuits, so the reader must be able to follow a wire or signal path from one drawing to the next. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.11

"This may be done in many ways, but generally the line or conductor to be continued will end at a terminal board." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.11

The board is labeled and numbered with the continuation drawing indicated. With no terminal board, the conductor should end with a number and the next drawing number. Some drawings add coordinates, and the second drawing refers back to the first. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.11

Block diagrams

Objectives 1.2

"Block diagrams are designed to present flow or functional information about the circuit or system, not detailed component data." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.12
"Whatever the block represents will be written inside." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.12
"The use of block diagrams is not restricted to electronic circuits." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.12

Block diagrams often accompany complex schematics, and show complex instrument channels and other systems when only the signal flowpath matters. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.12

Each block in this example is a stage in developing a signal that goes to the meter or to systems outside the drawing. Not all blocks are equal: some are several functions, and some are a single stage. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.13

"The creator of the block diagram decides the content of each block based on the intended use of the drawing." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.13
"In many cases, two or more types of drawings will be combined into a single print." DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.13

Figure 15 combines an electronic block diagram with an electrical single line, for part of the generator protection circuitry at a nuclear power generating plant. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.16

Worked examples

Objective 1.1

Read component values

Using this schematic, what are the values of R13 and C1?

  1. Find R13 and read the value printed beside it: 3.3K.
  2. Find C1 and read the value printed beside it: 50uf.

Answer: R13 is 3.3 kilo-ohm, or 3300 ohms. C1 is 50 microfarads, or 0.000050 farads.

DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.21

Objective 1.1

Identify numbered components

On the same schematic, which numbers mark the PNP transistor, the NPN transistor, the positive supply, the negative supply, the circuit ground, and the potentiometer?

  1. Check the transistor arrows for the numbers 1 and 2.
  2. Find the +15 volt and -15 volt supplies.
  3. Find the ground symbol and the part marked POT.

Answer: PNP transistor 2, NPN transistor 1, positive supply 7, negative supply 8, circuit ground 11, potentiometer 5.

DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.21

Objective 1.1

Decide if a transistor conducts

On the same schematic, the input to Q1 is at -15 volts. Will the transistor be conducting or nonconducting?

  1. Compare the base and the emitter potentials.
  2. The base (-15 v) is not positive relative to the emitter (-15 v).

Answer: Nonconducting.

DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.21

Objective 1.1

Count parts on a second schematic

How many resistors, transistors, and capacitors are in this circuit, and what is CR4?

  1. Count the resistors: R11, R13, R14, R20, R12, R1, and RL.
  2. Count Q2 and Q3, and read their type from the symbols.
  3. C7 is the only capacitor. CR4 has the diode symbol.

Answer: Seven resistors, two NPN transistors, one capacitor. CR4 is a diode.

DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.23

Summary

  • This chapter covered the common symbols for basic electronic components on diagrams, prints, and schematics. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.17
  • A block diagram presents the flow or functional information about a circuit, but it is not a detailed depiction of it. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.17
  • An electronic schematic diagram presents the detailed information about the circuit, each of its components, and how they are wired. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.17
  • The exercises practiced print reading on two electronic schematics. DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93 PR-04 p.23
